title: The Writing in the Crown: an Oroth fragment, with notes
author: transcribed inside the Cracked Toll; translation notes by Ismay Ondrael of the Circle
body:
# The Writing in the Crown

*Running around the inside of the crown of the Cracked Toll, where it is dark and a person would need a reason to be. Raised, not cut: it was in the mould. Transcribed by lamp. My notes are marked. — I. Ondrael*

---

**VAEL-OROTH · ANTHE SUL · HESK-MORN THAEL · ONDRAEL ISSE · CANTOR VAELETH · ORR**

---

## Notes

**VAEL-OROTH.** *Vael*, kept or held; *oroth*, the note, a held sound. "The Kept Note." This is the bell's name. Bells in Oroth work are named for what they are for, never for who paid, which by itself tells you a good deal about them.

**ANTHE SUL.** *Anthe*, choir, many voices; *sul*, light. "Choir-light," or, reading the compound the Oroth way with the modifier second, "the light of many voices." Sulion reads this as ornament. I read it as an instruction, because everything else in this line is an instruction.

**HESK-MORN THAEL.** *Hesk*, silence; *morn*, stone; *thael*, door. "The silent-stone door," or "the door of the silence-stone." There is a hinge-less door under Tollmere that opens for names. There is another at the Cantor's Seat. This bell is naming a door it is not standing next to, which either means the Builders labelled their works as a set, or that a bell is a door, and I am not prepared to write the second sentence out properly yet.

**ONDRAEL ISSE.** *Ondr*, deep; *isse*, water. "Deep water," or "the sunken deep." — I record, because it will be noticed and I would rather it were noticed by me: this is my own family name, which my mother's people took from an Oroth ruin above the Oskeld workings four generations ago, in the way people do. I have spent eleven years being careful about this line. It says deep water. It does not say anything about me.

**CANTOR VAELETH.** *Cantor*, the holder, the one who keeps the note — the Builders' title for an office, not a person, and never *our* word for a singer. *Vaeleth*: *vael*, to keep, with the participial *-eth*. "The Cantor is keeping," or "the holder holds," present and continuous.

Every other line on this bell is a name or an instruction. This one is a **status report**, cast into the inside of a bell in the Loud Age, where it could only be read by someone standing inside the finished object in the dark.

It was true when the bell was poured. On the evidence of the Order's vigil and of the hum in that bell as I write, it is true now.

**ORR.** *Orr* is bone. It is also, in the Skerrish that borrowed it, what is left when a thing is taken back but its weight is not.

One syllable, alone, at the end of a line of names and instructions. There is no verb. There is no article. A Sayer of my rank is expected to offer a reading.

I offer three and prefer none.

1. It is a maker's mark: the bell contains bone, which is possible; the clans salted giant-bone into bronze for a thousand years and the alloy rings longer.
2. It is the last word of a sentence that continues around a part of the crown that is no longer there, the bell being cracked.
3. It is the report's second half. *The holder holds. Bone.*

## On the tine

Found in a cradle of black stone in the crown, holding a half-step under the bell.

A fork holding a note under a bell is not decoration and is not a spare part. It is a **reference**. You do not tune a bell to a fork unless you expect the bell to drift, and you do not expect a bell to drift unless you expect the thing that is ringing it to change, and nothing was ringing this bell; it fell a thousand years ago and has been silent ever since.

It is humming now.

Either the reference has moved, or the world has, and there is a fork in a hillside in Hearthvale that has been waiting a thousand years to tell somebody which.

title: The Ash Winter: a chronicle in eleven hands
author: the chapter book of Pilgrim's Ash, Y.T. 866-867
body:
# The Ash Winter

*From the chapter book. Y.T. 866 to 867. The hands change where the hands changed; nobody could finish writing it at one sitting, and we have not tidied it, and we will not.*

---

**(first hand)** Cinderlea burned from the spring of 866. Not a forest fire; there is no forest. The ash heath burned, and under it the Builders' city burned, which nobody knew could burn, and the smoke went up for eleven months and the sun over Brightwater was the colour of a bad coin all that year.

We had grain from Tollmere at first. Then the roads west went under ash and the carts stopped coming.

**(second hand)** Greyfold did not starve. I want that written down by somebody who was there, because it is already being said in the north that they starved.

They had grain. They had a well. What they did not have was the sun, or a season, or any word from anywhere, for eleven months.

In the spring the ash stopped falling and they came out and looked at it, and the heath was grey, and the sky was grey, and a woman whose name I did not write down said: *it has finished here.*

**(third hand)** They laid the tables. That is the part strangers cannot get past and the part that is simplest. They laid the tables for a meal, all of them, every house, as if for a feast, and they left them laid, and they walked south singing.

They were not mad and they were not despairing. I stood in that lane and I watched and they were **tidy**. A man went back for a door he had left open. A girl of about twelve was counting them as they came out of the houses and telling her mother the number.

**(fourth hand)** Forty-one of us walked with them, out of the chapter tents, because you do not let people walk to the line alone.

**(fifth hand)** At the Choir the singing changed, or we heard it change. I will not say what it changed into because the four of us who have tried have written four different things.

We stopped at the ring. They went on.

**(sixth hand)** A voice from the Seat spoke to us at the ring and it used our names. All forty-one. It had not been told them.

It asked us to stay and keep count.

**(seventh hand)** Eleven stayed.

**(eighth hand)** I was one of the thirty who went on and I am writing this in the spring of 867 at Pilgrim's Ash, having turned back at the fortieth step of the stair, alone, in the grey, with no reason I can give.

Of the thirty, four came back. I have written the other twenty-six in the roll and I have written *went on* beside each, because I will not write *died*, having no evidence.

**(ninth hand)** The eleven who stayed kept count that first night and have kept it every night since. Four hundred and eleven bells, that first night. It is the oldest figure we have.

**(tenth hand)** We are asked, by the Circle and by the clans and by anyone who comes, what the voice was.

We do not know. We have four decades of bell-counts and no answer.

What we have instead is this: it knew forty-one names it had not been told, and it did not command, and it said *please*, which is in three of the eleven accounts and in none of the songs.

**(eleventh hand, much later and much shakier)** I was the girl who counted them coming out of the houses in Greyfold. Ninety-four.

I have been asked all my life how I am here and not there.

My mother put me on a cart. That is all. There is no mystery in it and there is no lesson in it and I have been a Toll-Knight for sixty years so that somebody who was there is still counting.

Ninety-four. Nobody else ever counted them. Write it in the roll.

title: A letter that was never sent
author: found folded under a laid table at Greyfold, addressed and not carried
body:
# A letter that was never sent

*Found folded under a plate at the third house on the lane at Greyfold, the table laid, the chairs pushed in. Addressed on the outside: 'To my sister at Gullhithe, by any hand going north.' There was no hand going north.*

---

Ellen,

The ash stopped this morning. Eleven months and it stopped in the night while we were asleep, which is a poor trick to play on people who have been listening to it.

We went out and looked. I will try to say it properly, because you always said I say things sideways.

It is grey. Not burnt — burnt has black in it and black is a colour. The heath is grey and the sky is the same grey and the line where they meet has gone. Tam held up his hand in front of his face and we all looked at his hand because it was the only thing in the world with a colour in it, and he laughed, and then he stopped.

We have grain. Write that down and show it to anybody who says otherwise afterwards: **we have grain, and the well is sweet.** Whatever is said about us, we did not starve.

What we have not had is one word from anywhere for eleven months. Not a cart, not a pedlar, not a light on the north road. You will say that is the ash and the roads, and it is, and there is a thing underneath that which I cannot put in a letter without sounding like the old women.

I will try. When nobody has said the name of your village for eleven months, you begin to feel that you are the one saying it, and that you are getting tired, and that when you stop nobody will take it up.

We are going south.

I know. I know what you will say and I have said it to myself in your voice for a fortnight. Here is the answer, such as it is: it has finished here, and we would rather walk than sit in it and go quiet by inches with the table laid and nobody coming.

We are laying the tables. That was Mother Oss's idea and everyone took it up, and I thought it was a dreadful piece of theatre and I have changed my mind. A house left tidy for a meal is a house somebody expects to come back to, and if we are wrong about all of it — if in the spring the carts come and the sun is the right colour — then somebody will find nine houses laid for supper and will know we were not mad, and will sit down.

So: if you come, sit down and eat. I mean that. The plates are for whoever.

The grey knights from the tents are walking with us as far as the ring. They are very kind and they do not argue and they sing badly.

Tell the Lamp keeper her light is the last thing we could see from the north field for the whole of the ash, on the clear nights, going round and round. I do not think she knows what that was worth and I could not have written it without sounding foolish and I am past that now.

Say my name sometimes, Ellen. Not for grief. Just say it in the ordinary way, to whoever is there, the way you used to say it when you were cross with me.

There is no hand going north. I am going to fold this and put it under my plate, which is the last stupid thing I shall do, and then we are going.

Your sister,
Annet

title: The Briar Keeps Out: a plain answer to a foolish pamphlet
author: the Sayers' Circle, Tollmere, published at the Spire
body:
# The Briar Keeps Out

*Published at the Spire in answer to a pamphlet circulating in Isseva and the Wold, which is wrong, and which is wrong in a way that will get somebody killed.*

The Thornmarch was grown by the Builders along the eastern rim in about the year −900 to keep something **out**.

The evidence is not complicated and it is not contested by anyone who has read the Oroth.

**First: the geometry.** A wall is built on the side you are defending. The Briar's densest growth, its thickest stems and its deepest rooting, is on the western face — our face. Its outer face is thinner, older and unmaintained. You do not armour the inside of a cage. You armour the inside of a **shield**.

**Second: the gates.** There are four. They are on our side, they are wide enough for a cart, and they were maintained for nine hundred years by somebody. A prison with four cart-gates on the prisoner's side is not a prison. We are being asked to believe the Builders locked the Dwindling in behind a door with a handle.

**Third: the Oroth.** *Thael* is door. *Hesk* is silence. The wardstones at the four gates carry the same line: HESK-THAEL VAEL — "the silence-door, kept." Kept, held, maintained. It is the language of a garrison and not of a gaol.

**Fourth, and we would rather not have to say it.** The pamphlet's author has never been east of the Briar. We have. The Circle sent two Listeners and a chart-maker through the northern gate in 1038. They walked four days east along a road of fused stone, straight as a rule, and they came back, and their report is in the Spire library and may be read by anyone who asks and nobody does.

There is a road. It goes east for a hundred miles. At the end of it, on their chart, there is a second ring of towers.

The Dwindling is not east. The Dwindling is **south**, behind us, where the Hushline is, where the colour goes out of a man's hands, where there is no wall at all and never has been.

## Why this matters now

The grey patches in the Briar are spreading. The foresters count them; fourteen at midwinter, nineteen now.

If the wall is a shield, a hole in it is a breach, and what is on the other side of a breach comes through it. Ash-wights have been found at the Breach, four regions from Cinderlea, wandering in a wood where nothing of the kind has ever been recorded.

The pamphlet's answer to this is that the wights *escaped*, which requires them to have walked from Cinderlea across two regions and a lake to reach the one gap in a wall they were supposedly inside.

Ours is that they came from the east along a road with a second Seat at the end of it.

We may be wrong. We have been wrong before and we publish our errors, which is more than the Wold does.

But the two accounts give opposite instructions, and instructions are what a pamphlet is for. Ours: **mend the wall**. Theirs: **open it**.

One of us is asking the foresters to do something that cannot be undone.

title: The Briar Keeps In: what the Wold knows and the Spire does not
author: set down at Fernhold from the Sedgish songs and thirty years of walking the wall
body:
# The Briar Keeps In

*The Circle has published a plain answer to me. I am obliged to it; it has saved me the trouble of stating its case. Here is mine, and I have walked this wall every morning for thirty years, which is not an argument, and I mention it anyway.*

The Thornmarch was grown to keep the Dwindling **in**, in the south and east, where it had already begun.

## On their four points

**The geometry.** They say the western face is thicker, so we are the defended side. I say the western face is thicker because for nine hundred years the Woodfolk have cut, laid and tended it from the west, that being the side we live on, and the Circle has mistaken thirty generations of hedging for Builders' intent. Come and look. The laying is ours. The knots are ours. My grandmother's work is eleven miles of it.

**The gates.** Four gates, wide, on our side. Yes. And every one of them faces a **Hearthstone**, and every one of them has a wardstone reading HESK-THAEL VAEL, and the Circle translates *vael* as "kept" and stops there.

*Vael* is kept, held, **not let go of**. It is the word in CANTOR VAELETH, on the inside of their own Cracked Toll: the holder holds. It is the word for what a fist does. If the four gates say anything, they say: this door is held shut, and here is a stone where you may be named so that you are still yourself when you come back through it.

**The eastern road.** I believe their chart-maker. I believe there is a road and a second ring of towers a hundred miles east.

I ask the Circle a question they have not answered in five years of pamphlets: **what is the second ring for?**

Theirs is the account in which the Builders raised Harmonies everywhere to hold the world's note. Very well. Then a second Seat at the end of a straight road is not a threat to be walled out. It is another one of theirs, and the Briar does not run between us and it — the Briar runs *around* both, and we are inside the same wall as the thing they are afraid of, and have been for nine hundred years, and nothing has come down that road in all that time.

**The wights at the Breach.** They walked. The Circle finds this absurd because they have never watched one. They are slow and they are stupid and they never stop, and two regions in a hundred and seventy years is a stroll.

## What the songs say

The Sedgish have a round about the raising of the wall. They have had it longer than Tollmere has had a charter, and it says the Builders grew the thorn *after* the wrong note, in a hurry, and that they grew it the wrong way round on purpose, so that people would tend it from the inside and never ask.

## What I am actually asking for

Not to open the wall. I have never asked that and the Circle knows it.

I am asking that when it fails — and it is failing, nineteen patches and counting, and it will not be mended by a foresters' lodge with billhooks — we do not spend the last of it patching the east and watching the wrong horizon.

The grey is coming from the south. It has always been coming from the south. The wall was grown to give us time, and we have had nine hundred years of it, and the Circle has spent the last five arguing about which way a hedge faces.

— *Alder Wyke, forester, Fernhold*
